Speed bin distributions from FleetDNA parcel delivery vocation of single-unit short-haul by hour 5.1.2 CE-CERT Speed Distributions for Source Type and Vocation by Hour From Section 4: Data Density, categories with insufficient data are grayed out and not graphed, categories that have low vehicle counts or little recorded driving time are shaded in pale orange, and caution should be exercised when analyzing these results. Data files for this section are saved under the name SpeedDistributionResults_byHour_source_cecert.csv and SpeedDistributionResults_byHour_vocation_cecert.csv for source types and vocations, respectively. Figure 28 shows the speed bin distributions for the combination-unit short-haul source type when there is sufficient data from CE-CERT. Hourly lines are a little more sporadic for the low-data categories (pale orange background), but in general we see a main 60-mph peak on freeways and 5 mph on other roads. Other roads also have some minor peaks at 15 mph and 60 mph for the early morning hours on weekdays. On weekends, other roads have some minor peaks for afternoon hours at 15 and 20 mph and for morning hours at 35 and 45 mph. 38 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Speed bin distributions for CE-CERT combination-unit short-haul vehicles by hour Figure 29 shows the speed distributions for the single-unit short-haul source type from the CE- CERT data set. On urban freeways, early morning and late-night hours have a flat peak between 50 and 55 mph, while hours around midday tend to be peaking slightly faster at 55 to 60 mph. Freeway work and street sweeper vehicles may perform work during midnight hours and comprise the slightly slower peak. 39 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 29. Speed bin distributions for CE-CERT single-unit short-haul vehicles by hour Figure 30 and Figure 31 display the speed distributions for freeway work trucks and street sweepers, respectively. For vehicles of both vocations, we see a peak at 50 mph on weekdays and 55 mph for weekends. Other vocations had some proportion spent at these speeds, but their peaks were not as pronounced as these two.
